Cache strategies

Caches are the difference between a 30-second warm build and a 5-minute cold one. gocdnext’s cache: block tars listed paths at job end, stores them in the cache backend (the artefact store), and restores them at the start of the next job that asks for the same key.

The block

Two parts:

  • key: — the cache name. Two runs with the same resolved key share the cache entry.
  • paths: — directories OR files to tar. Glob patterns supported.

Key templating

There is one template token in the cache key grammar:

TokenExpansion
{{ hash "<glob>" }}hex digest of the sorted files matching the glob (workspace-relative).

The agent’s cache resolver expands {{ hash }} tokens before fetching/storing — content-keyed caches “just work”:

Bump the lockfile → digest changes → new cache bucket. Older buckets age out via the retention sweeper.

The glob is workspace-relative with no .. traversal. A glob that matches zero files aborts the job rather than silently producing an empty hash. Limits: ≤ 100 files matched, ≤ 16 MiB per file, ≤ 64 MiB total — set generously to make the audit trail predictable.

Shell-style ${VAR} is NOT expanded in cache keys

Cache keys are passed to the storage backend verbatim. The agent does not run shell-style variable expansion on them (${CI_BRANCH}, ${CI_PIPELINE_NAME}, etc. stay as literal text). So this:

becomes the literal storage key pnpm-store-${CI_BRANCH} — every branch shares the same bucket. That’s fine for most caches (pnpm store, Go mod cache, Maven .m2) because the contents are content-addressable and multi-version-safe; cohabitation is the whole design.

You rarely need per-branch keys, because writes are already isolated per ref — see below.

Branch isolation (PR-safe scoping)

Even when every branch resolves to the same key, their cache writes never clobber each other. The server scopes each write to a ref lane, GitHub-Actions style — automatically, with nothing to configure in the pipeline:

  • A push / integration to the project default branch writes the shared lane (@).
  • Every other ref — feature-branch push, pull request, merge queue, tag — writes its own isolated lane and reads its own lane first, then falls back to the shared lane as a base.

So a pull request restores the default branch’s cache (warm start), then saves its own additions to a private lane. A second PR running concurrently can’t overwrite the first’s cache or the default branch’s — the clobbering that produced “cache hit but still a dependency miss” under a single shared blob is gone.

Why this matters for additive caches (Gradle’s build cache, in particular): the blob is replaced whole on each write, but task outputs accumulate. Before scoping, two PRs restoring the same key, each adding their own entries, raced — the last writer’s blob overwrote the others, so the next run missed entries that were computed. Per-lane writes remove the race: each ref owns its blob.

This is a server policy; pipelines don’t opt in and there’s no YAML field. Operators see the lane per row under Project → Caches (“default” = the shared lane).

What to cache (by toolchain)

Node / pnpm

Plugin sets pnpm config store-dir /workspace/.pnpm-store so the content-addressable store lives in the workspace. node_modules/ also caches the resolved tree so install is just a verify pass.

Go

Plugin redirects GOMODCACHE=/workspace/.go-mod and GOCACHE=/workspace/.go-cache. Both matter — .go-mod is fetched modules, .go-cache is compiled package artefacts (incremental builds + memoised test results).

Maven

Plugin redirects the local repository to /workspace/.m2. A typical 200-dep project lands at 200-500 MB.

Gradle

Two paths because Gradle has TWO independent caches: GRADLE_USER_HOME (deps) and the build cache (--build-cache, task-output memo). Cache both for full warmth.

For the build cache specifically there’s a better option than tarring the whole directory — see Embedded Gradle build cache below. Keep the cache: block for GRADLE_USER_HOME (deps); point --build-cache at the embedded remote cache.

Python (uv)

uv writes its package cache to .cache/uv/ when run from /workspace. The resolved venv at .venv/ should also travel — restoring it skips the resolver.

Python (Poetry)

Plugin sets POETRY_VIRTUALENVS_IN_PROJECT=1 so .venv is local and POETRY_CACHE_DIR=/workspace/.cache/pypoetry so the wheel cache is in the workspace.

trivy (security DB)

Trivy’s vulnerability DB is the cached artefact, not anything project-derived — use a constant key so all projects share the warm DB. Pair with skip-db-update: "true" on air-gapped agents.

Docker buildx

buildx layer caches go through buildx’s own cache backends, not the platform’s cache: block. Use the plugin’s cache:/ cache-from:/cache-to: inputs:

The platform’s cache: block is for filesystem dirs; buildx’s layer cache is content-addressable in the registry, which the platform doesn’t mediate. See the layer-cache recipe for the runner-profile pattern.

Embedded Gradle build cache

The cache: block tars a whole directory and stores it under one key. That’s the right model for a dependency store (pnpm, .m2, GRADLE_USER_HOME), but it’s a mismatch for Gradle’s build cache, which is entry-addressable: each task output is keyed by a hash of its inputs. gocdnext can serve Gradle’s build cache natively — it implements the Gradle HTTP build cache protocol, so each task output is one object keyed by its hash.

Why this is better than tarring the build-cache dir:

  • Entry-level sharing. Two branches/PRs that compute the same task output share the same entry (same input hash → same key).
  • No clobbering, ever. Entries are immutable and idempotent — concurrent writers of the same key write identical bytes.
  • No whole-dir transfer. A build fetches only the entries it needs and pushes only new ones.
  • No extra service. It’s an endpoint on the gocdnext server, backed by the same object store. The handler is stateless, so scale it with server replicas. (Entry bytes are proxied through the server: Gradle’s cache client rejects HTTP redirects, so a signed-URL redirect isn’t an option.)

Enable it

In Project → Settings → Gradle build cache (or POST /api/v1/projects/{slug}/build-cache/token), click Enable. That generates a project token (shown once; only its hash is stored).

Jobs that use the gradle plugin are then wired automatically — the server injects the cache URL + a short-lived, per-run token into the job’s env (the token is masked in logs), and the plugin drops a Gradle init script that points HttpBuildCache at gocdnext. Nothing to add to your repo; just run the build.

Auto-wiring needs the operator to set a signing key on the server (GOCDNEXT_BUILD_CACHE_SIGN_KEY, hex) — without it, the manual path below still works.

Manual setup (non-plugin builds)

For a build that doesn’t use the gradle plugin, point Gradle at the cache yourself in settings.gradle.kts (the rotate response gives you this snippet pre-filled).

Caution

The static project token is read/write and has no ref awareness — anyone who can present it can push. The read-only-for-PRs guarantee only applies to the auto-wired (gradle-plugin) path, where the server mints a per-run token scoped to the run’s ref. If you use the static token, give it only to trusted (default-branch) builds — store it as a secret that PR jobs can’t read. Prefer the auto-wired path when you can.

Run with --build-cache (or org.gradle.caching=true). Keep the cache: block for GRADLE_USER_HOME (dependencies); the embedded cache handles the task-output build cache.

The token authenticates the build (HTTP Basic) and scopes it to one project — a token for project A can’t read or write project B’s entries. Rotating or disabling the token is immediate (a disable revokes outstanding auto-wired tokens too).

Only default-branch builds write; PRs and feature branches are read-only. Auto-wired PR/branch runs get a read-only token (push off), so an untrusted run can read the default branch’s entries but can’t poison the shared cache or exhaust its storage — the same trust model as PR-safe scoping. A single entry PUT is capped (GOCDNEXT_BUILD_CACHE_MAX_ENTRY_MB, default 512). Entry bytes are proxied through the server (Gradle’s cache client doesn’t follow redirects); the handler is stateless, so scale reads with server replicas.

Eviction

Entries are immutable objects in the bucket. For now, bound growth with an object-store lifecycle rule on the gradle-cache/ prefix (e.g. “delete objects older than N days”) — a content- addressed cache tolerates this: a deleted entry is just recomputed. Server-tracked, last-access-based eviction is planned.

Eviction

Caches age out. The retention sweeper runs every tick and:

  1. Drops entries whose last_accessed_at is past the configured TTL. The shared (default-branch) lane uses the long horizon (default 30 days, caches.ttlDays in Helm); the isolated per-ref lanes use a shorter one (default 7 days, caches.scopedTtlDays) so a merged or abandoned branch’s cache surrenders disk fast instead of multiplying with branch churn. A PR reading the shared lane bumps its freshness, so the default branch’s cache never ages out from under active PRs.
  2. Drops oldest entries when a project exceeds its quota (caches.projectQuotaBytes).
  3. Drops oldest entries globally when the total exceeds the global quota (caches.globalQuotaBytes).
  4. Reclaims rows stuck in pending past a grace window (an agent that requested an upload slot and died before finalising it). Per-ref lanes make these accumulate with branch churn, so the sweep bounds the leak.

What “oldest” means: LRU on last_accessed_at. Caches that get hit on every push survive forever; abandoned project caches age out within a month.

last_accessed_at is updated whenever a job restores from the cache, so an active project on a feature branch keeps that hash-key’s cache warm even if main hasn’t touched it in weeks.

Operators can also purge caches manually via Project → Caches in the dashboard.

Pre-warming + invalidation

Pre-warm

When you bump a lockfile, the first run with the new hash key hits a cold cache. That’s expected — the cost amortises over subsequent runs against the same hash.

For projects with very long install times, pre-warm by triggering a Run latest on the new lockfile state ahead of merging the bump PR.

Invalidate when something changes the resolution

{{ hash "lockfile" }} invalidates automatically. For caches keyed on a constant string, force-invalidate by bumping the key:

The retention sweeper drops the old pnpm-store entries on its quota pass.

Common pitfalls

  • Caching the wrong path: Maven’s .m2/ outside /workspace is the system default — agents can’t see it. The plugins REDIRECT into the workspace; if you bypass the plugin (use image: maven:3.9 + script: directly), set MAVEN_OPTS= -Dmaven.repo.local=/workspace/.m2 yourself.
  • Cache size growth: Gradle’s build cache can hit 5+ GiB on big multi-module projects. Set caches.projectQuotaBytes in Helm to bound; LRU eviction trims when needed.
  • Cache corruption: a flaky agent can write a partial tar. The cache restore pass treats a failed restore as a miss, wipes the partially-extracted paths, and proceeds to a cold install. The corrupt entry stays around until quota / TTL evicts it. Symptom: random “missing dependency” errors that disappear on the next run — clear the cache via the dashboard if you suspect this.
  • “Cache hit but still a dependency miss” across concurrent PRs: was caused by branches clobbering one shared blob. Fixed by PR-safe scoping — each ref writes its own lane now. If you still see it, confirm the task’s inputs aren’t PR-specific (e.g. a per-build -Drevision baked into a compile task’s hash poisons the build-cache key itself).
  • Shell-style vars in key:: ${CI_BRANCH} (and friends) stay LITERAL in cache keys — they don’t expand. Use {{ hash }} for content-keyed caches; use constant strings otherwise.
